title: Isles of Scilly
description: Group of islands in Cornwall, England
wiki_lead:
The Isles of Scilly (, SIL-ee; Cornish: Syllan) are a small archipelago in Cornwall, England, approximately 45 km (28 mi) south-west of Land's End. One of the islands, St Agnes, is over four miles (six kilometres) further south than the most southerly point of the British mainland at Lizard Point, and has the southernmost inhabited settlement in Cornwall and the UK, Troy Town.
The total population of the islands at the 2021 United Kingdom census was 2,100. A majority live on one island, St Mary's, and close to half live in Hugh Town; the remainder live on four inhabited "off-islands".
People have lived on the islands since at least the Iron Age, and the Romans knew them as Sillina. Rising sea levels flooded low-lying land, and the islands were probably once much larger, possibly a single island. In the Middle Ages they belonged to Tavistock Abbey, which founded a priory on Tresco. During the English Civil War they were a Royalist base until Parliament captured them in 1651. In 1707, four Royal Navy ships were wrecked off the islands, and at least 1,450 people died. Most of the islands were held on lease, first by the Godolphin family and later by the Smith family, until 1920, when they passed back to the Duchy of Cornwall.
The islands are known for pilot gig racing, a rowing sport that began with crews racing to put pilots on ships. The World Pilot Gig Championships are held there every year over the May Day bank holiday weekend. The islands have what is reportedly the world's smallest football league. A 2006 survey found that residents were the most active in England for sport and fitness. Rock climbing and bouldering on the granite coast have been practised since 1977. The islands have also featured on television, including in the BBC series An Island Parish.
Scilly forms part of the ceremonial county of Cornwall and was historically one of the hundreds of Cornwall. Since 1890, the islands have had their own local authority, the Council of the Isles of Scilly, which is administratively separate from the mainland Cornwall Council, although some services are provided by it.
The adjective "Scillonian" is sometimes used for people or things related to the archipelago. The Duchy of Cornwall owns most of the freehold land on the islands. Tourism is a major part of the local economy along with agriculture, particularly the production of cut flowers.

Name
Scilly was known to the Romans as Sil(l)ina, a Latinisation of a Brittonic name that became Cornish Sillan, or Syllan in modern spelling. The name is of unknown origin, but has been speculatively linked to the goddess Sulis. The English name Scilly first appeared in 1176, in the form Sully. The unetymological c was added in the 16th century in order to distinguish the name from the word "silly", whose meaning was shifting at this time from "happy" to "foolish".

grok_lead: The Isles of Scilly constitute an archipelago of approximately 200 low-lying granite islands and rocks covering 1,600 hectares, positioned about 45 kilometres southwest of Land's End in the Atlantic Ocean off the Cornish peninsula. Only five islands are permanently inhabitedâSt Mary's, Tresco, St Martin's, Bryher, and St Agnesâwith the total resident population numbering around 2,300, the majority concentrated on St Mary's, the principal island featuring the main harbour and airfield. Administered separately from mainland Cornwall as England's smallest unitary authority by the Council of the Isles of Scilly, established in 1891 with powers equivalent to those of county councils, the islands exhibit a mild oceanic climate conducive to subtropical vegetation and lack of frost, supporting an economy centred on tourism, commercial flower production, and inshore fishing. Designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty since 1951, the Isles attract visitors for their unspoiled beaches, diverse wildlife including seabird colonies, and prehistoric monuments, while their remote location and granite geology contribute to a history marked by numerous shipwrecks and strategic military significance.
